quickStart.title: Quick Start
quickStart.body: For first-time setup, complete the flow in this order: add a provider, create a key and pool, bind the key to the pool, then configure Codex.
items: Add a provider: choose OpenAI Responses or the matching platform on the home page, add an upstream provider, then fill in Base URL, API Key, protocol endpoint, and model settings.
Create a key: open the Keys page and generate a Relay Key. The full key is shown only once, so copy and store it immediately.
Create a pool and bind the key: return to Provider Pools, create a pool, choose members and mode, then bind the Relay Key to that pool.
Configure the pool: use managed mode for auto-selection, retry, and fallback; use manual mode to pin traffic to one provider. Make sure pool members are enabled.
Configure Codex: point Codex Base URL to the Code Switch OpenAI/Codex relay address, use the Relay Key as the API key, then enable OpenAI Responses hosting.

overview.title: Overview
overview.body: Code Switch centralizes providers, relay keys, and diagnostics for Claude Code, Codex/OpenAI Responses, and OpenAI Chat.
items: The home page groups providers and provider pools by platform; use the top tabs to switch platforms.
When hosting is enabled, the local relay takes over the matching CLI API traffic and chooses providers from your configuration.
Settings, Keys, Logs, and Console cover system configuration, access control, request tracing, and runtime debugging.

providers.title: Providers
providers.body: A provider is an upstream API configuration with a name, base URL, API key, protocol endpoints, model whitelist, model mapping, and optional availability checks.
items: Open a provider tab and add a provider, then fill in the API Base URL, API Key, and protocol endpoint.
Use the model whitelist to declare supported models, and model mapping to translate CLI model names to upstream model names.
Enabled providers can participate in hosted traffic; disabled providers keep their configuration but are skipped by routing.

pools.title: Pools
pools.body: Pools combine multiple providers into one routing unit for automatic selection, retry, and fallback.
items: Create a pool from the Provider Pools view, then choose managed mode or manual mode.
Managed mode lets enabled providers in the pool participate in auto-selection, retries, and fallback.
Manual mode uses only the selected provider, which is useful for debugging or a temporary fixed upstream.

keys.title: Keys
keys.body: The Keys page manages API keys for Code Switch Relay. Clients must use generated keys when calling the local or server relay.
items: The full key is shown only once after creation; save it immediately because later views only show a masked value.
You can rename and delete keys, then inspect calls and token usage across time ranges.
Create separate keys per device, project, or automation job to simplify auditing and revocation.

binding.title: Binding Keys to Pools
binding.body: After a key is bound to a pool, requests made with that key are routed according to that pool's provider rules.
items: Open the Provider Pools view and bind an unbound key from the pool card.
Bound keys appear in the pool's key list and can be unbound at any time.
Keys without a bound pool use the current platform default behavior; separate bindings isolate teams, projects, or environments.

logs.title: Logs
logs.body: The Logs page shows active relay requests and up to 105 recent completed records.
items: Queued, processing, and retrying requests refresh from memory and appear above each completed-record page.
Completed records are limited to the latest 105 at 15 per page; platform and provider remain visible as table columns.
Relay key, model, HTTP status, first-token latency, and duration help identify whether an issue is in the client, relay, or upstream.

console.title: Console
console.body: The Console shows application runtime output for diagnosing relay startup, config writes, upstream connectivity, and backend service errors.
items: If hosting does not enable, a provider cannot be saved, or a CLI cannot connect, check the latest console errors first.
Console output complements request logs: logs explain individual requests, while the console explains application state.
Clear the console after debugging when you want to watch only the output from the next operation.

codex.title: Configuring Codex
codex.body: Codex/OpenAI Responses traffic is routed through the local relay, usually from the OpenAI Responses tab and the Keys page.
items: Add a provider under OpenAI Responses, including upstream Base URL, API Key, Responses endpoint, and model configuration.
Generate a Relay Key, then configure Codex with the Code Switch OpenAI/Codex relay Base URL and that Relay Key as the API key.
Enable hosting for OpenAI Responses; bind the Relay Key to a specific pool when you need project-level routing isolation.

codeBlocks.label: Write ~/.codex/config.toml
codeBlocks.code:
model = "gpt-5.5"
model_provider = "wcisman"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"
preferred_auth_method = 'apikey'


[model_providers.wcisman]
base_url = "https://api.wcisman.cc"
name = 'codex'
requires_openai_auth = true
wire_api = 'responses'

settings.title: Settings and Security
settings.body: Settings cover appearance, startup, notifications, admin security, and availability monitoring.
items: The admin UI and relay listen on localhost by default; use Caddy or Nginx as an HTTPS reverse proxy for public deployments.
Security settings manage admin sign-in and sessions; use strong credentials for public deployments.
Availability monitoring can check providers periodically, and auto-blacklist reduces the impact of unavailable upstreams.
